option_description: Controls the mutual TLS enforcement mode across the service mesh for all service-to-service communication. STRICT mode requires valid X.509 client certificates on every connection; PERMISSIVE accepts both plaintext and mTLS traffic simultaneously; DISABLED allows only plaintext. This is typically set via PeerAuthentication resources in Istio or equivalent mesh-level configuration.
security_impact: The Rego policy for mutual_tls_enforcement_coverage requires `input.mtls_mode == 'STRICT'` as a mandatory condition. If the value is PERMISSIVE or DISABLED, the countermeasure does not activate, meaning unauthenticated lateral communication paths remain open within the cluster. PERMISSIVE mode is a common migration aid that becomes a persistent misconfiguration when never promoted to STRICT, leaving services vulnerable to interception and impersonation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all PeerAuthentication policies across every namespace to inspect the mTLS mode setting for each
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get peerauthentication --all-namespaces -o yaml | grep -A5 'spec:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: YAML blocks showing spec.mtls.mode values; STRICT indicates full enforcement, PERMISSIVE or absence of the field indicates weaker posture

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for the mesh-wide root PeerAuthentication policy in the Istio control plane namespace specifically
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get peerauthentication -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.mtls.mode}{"\n"}{end}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output listing policy names and their mode; expect 'STRICT' for compliant deployments

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Linkerd mesh environments, verify that mTLS is enforced by checking the control plane configuration and server authorization resources
how_to_obtain.command: linkerd check --proxy && kubectl get serverauthorization --all-namespaces -o yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Healthy proxy check output and ServerAuthorization objects that restrict unauthenticated traffic

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the Kiali service mesh observability console, navigate to the Istio Config section and filter by PeerAuthentication resources to visually inspect mTLS mode per namespace
how_to_obtain.navigation: Kiali Dashboard > Istio Config > PeerAuthentication > inspect 'mtls.mode' column for all entries
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Table view showing STRICT mode for all namespaces with no PERMISSIVE or DISABLED entries

option_description: Indicates whether a single root PeerAuthentication policy (or equivalent) is deployed in the mesh control plane namespace to enforce mTLS across all services and namespaces globally. Without this, enforcement depends entirely on per-service or per-namespace policies, which can leave newly deployed services unenforced by default until explicitly configured.
security_impact: The Rego mutual_tls_enforcement_coverage rule requires `input.mesh_wide_policy_enforced == true` alongside STRICT mode and a configured CA. A mesh-wide policy acts as a security backstop — even if a new namespace or workload is deployed without an explicit PeerAuthentication, the root policy ensures mTLS is still required. Without it, onboarding gaps and human error create windows where services communicate in plaintext.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for the presence of a root PeerAuthentication policy in the istio-system namespace that applies mesh-wide with STRICT mode
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get peerauthentication -n istio-system -o yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A PeerAuthentication resource with no selector (applying to all workloads) and spec.mtls.mode set to STRICT; absence of such a resource means the attribute is false

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that the policy has no workload selector (meaning it applies globally) and confirm STRICT mode is set
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get peerauthentication -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.selector}{"\t"}{.spec.mtls.mode}{"\n"}{end}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rows where selector is empty/null and mode is STRICT confirm a true mesh-wide policy

how_to_obtain.instruction: If using Helm-deployed Istio, review the values file to check if meshConfig or global mTLS settings were set to enforce STRICT at installation time
how_to_obtain.command: helm get values istio-base -n istio-system
how_to_obtain.file_path: istio-operator values.yaml or IstioOperator custom resource
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Fields such as meshConfig.enableAutoMtls: true and global.mtls.enabled: true indicate mesh-wide enforcement was configured at install

option_description: Indicates whether a certificate authority is actively running and issuing workload X.509 certificates (SVIDs or equivalent) to mesh-injected sidecars. This is the foundational requirement for any cryptographic service identity — without a functioning CA, mTLS cannot be established regardless of policy configuration.
security_impact: The Rego mutual_tls_enforcement_coverage rule requires `input.certificate_authority_configured == true`. Even with STRICT PeerAuthentication policies in place, if the CA is not issuing certificates to workload sidecars, all mTLS handshakes will fail and services will be unable to communicate — or worse, fall back to plaintext if misconfigured. A healthy CA is the trust anchor for the entire zero-trust service mesh model.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that the istiod control plane pod is running and that the Istio CA secret is present in the istio-system namespace
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod && kubectl get secret istio-ca-secret -n istio-system
how_to_obtain.expected_output: istiod pod in Running state and the istio-ca-secret secret existing with non-empty certificate data

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm that a sample workload sidecar has received a valid certificate by inspecting its certificate via the Envoy admin interface
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl exec -n <namespace> <pod-name> -c istio-proxy -- pilot-agent request GET certs
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output listing certificate chain details including SPIFFE URI SAN (e.g., spiffe://cluster.local/ns/<ns>/sa/<sa>) with a valid validity period

how_to_obtain.instruction: For SPIRE deployments, verify that the SPIRE server is running and that registered workload entries are present
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -n spire && kubectl exec -n spire spire-server-0 -- /opt/spire/bin/spire-server entry show
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SPIRE server pod running and a list of workload registration entries with SPIFFE IDs mapped to Kubernetes service accounts

how_to_obtain.instruction: For cert-manager based PKI, check that ClusterIssuer or Issuer resources are in Ready state
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterissuer,issuer --all-namespaces -o wide
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Issuer resources showing READY=True status; any False or Unknown state indicates CA configuration issues

option_description: Identifies the system responsible for issuing cryptographic credentials (X.509 certificates or bound tokens) to individual service workloads. Options include SPIFFE/SPIRE for federated workload identity, Istio's built-in Citadel/istiod CA, cloud-provider workload identity systems (AWS IRSA, GCP Workload Identity), custom PKI infrastructure, or none if no dedicated identity system is configured.
security_impact: The Rego service_identity_verification_accuracy rule checks that `input.workload_identity_provider` is not in the 'none' list. Without a dedicated workload identity provider, services cannot be cryptographically distinguished from one another — a compromised service could impersonate any other service. Strong providers like SPIFFE/SPIRE issue SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Documents (SVIDs) tied to platform attestation, making identity spoofing computationally infeasible.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check if SPIRE is deployed in the cluster by looking for the spire-server and spire-agent pods
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces | grep -E 'spire|spiffe'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Running spire-server and spire-agent pods indicate spiffe_spire as the provider

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify whether Istio's built-in istiod CA (Citadel) is serving as the identity provider by checking the istiod service and certificate configuration
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get configmap istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | grep -E 'ca|citadel|trustDomain'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: trustDomain and CA configuration fields confirm istio_citadel as provider; presence of caAddress pointing to external service indicates custom_pki

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS EKS environments, check for IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) configuration via pod annotations and OIDC provider
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[].spec.serviceAccountName' | sort -u && aws eks describe-cluster --name <cluster-name> --query 'cluster.identity.oidc'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: OIDC issuer URL present in cluster configuration and pods with eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn annotation indicate cloud_iam_workload_identity

how_to_obtain.instruction: For GCP GKE environments, verify Workload Identity binding by checking service account annotations and node pool configuration
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get serviceaccounts --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.metadata.annotations["iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account"] != null) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Service accounts with GCP IAM annotation confirm cloud_iam_workload_identity; no matching annotations alongside no SPIRE/istiod suggests none

option_description: Controls whether Kubernetes pods are configured to use projected service account tokens — short-lived, audience-bound JWT tokens that are automatically rotated and cryptographically tied to a specific service account, cluster, and time window. This replaces long-lived static tokens mounted by default in older Kubernetes versions.
security_impact: The Rego service_identity_verification_accuracy rule includes a condition checking `input.service_account_token_projection_enabled == true` as an alternative or complementary path to workload identity provider verification. Projected tokens provide a mechanism to cryptographically bind a service's identity to outbound requests with a constrained TTL. Static or long-lived tokens are high-value targets since they remain valid indefinitely after exfiltration, while projected tokens expire quickly and cannot be used outside their intended audience scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check pod specs across namespaces for projected volume mounts of type serviceAccountToken with explicit audience and expirationSeconds settings
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.volumes[]?.projected.sources[]?.serviceAccountToken != null) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name, tokenConfig: .spec.volumes[].projected.sources[]?.serviceAccountToken}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pod entries showing serviceAccountToken projected volumes with expirationSeconds (typically 3600) and audience fields confirm the feature is enabled

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the kube-apiserver configuration to verify that the BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume feature gate is enabled (default in Kubernetes 1.21+)
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pod -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver -o yaml | grep -E 'feature-gates|BoundServiceAccount'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume=true in feature gates, or its absence in 1.21+ where it is enabled by default

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review service account or pod security admission configuration for projected token requirements in namespace labels or pod admission policies
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get namespace --show-labels | grep -E 'pod-security|token'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Namespaces with pod security standards enforcing projected token usage; check admission webhook configurations for token projection requirements

how_to_obtain.instruction: Examine a running pod's mounted token to confirm it is a projected token (JWT with exp claim and audience) rather than a legacy static token
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl exec -n <namespace> <pod-name> -- cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | jq '{aud, exp, iss}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JWT payload showing 'aud' field with specific audience value and 'exp' claim with near-future expiry; absence of exp or generic audience indicates legacy static token

option_description: Indicates whether AuthorizationPolicy resources (Istio), ServerAuthorization objects (Linkerd), or equivalent mesh-level access control objects are deployed that explicitly restrict which source service principals are permitted to invoke specific destination services. This enforces least-privilege at the network level independent of application-layer authentication.
security_impact: The Rego authorization_policy_granularity rule has `input.authorization_policies_deployed == true` as its foundational prerequisite condition — without it, no further authorization granularity evaluation can occur. Without AuthorizationPolicies, even a fully STRICT mTLS mesh only provides encryption and mutual authentication; any authenticated service can call any other service. Authorization policies complete the zero-trust model by enforcing what authenticated services are permitted to do, limiting lateral movement blast radius in the event of a service compromise.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all AuthorizationPolicy resources across every namespace to confirm policies exist and identify their scope
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy --all-namespaces -o wide
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Table listing AuthorizationPolicy resources per namespace with their action (ALLOW/DENY); absence of any entries means the attribute is false

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the content of existing AuthorizationPolicies to verify they bind source principals (service account or namespace-based selectors) to destination services
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name, action: .spec.action, sources: [.spec.rules[]?.from[]?.source]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output showing policies with 'from' sources referencing principals or namespaces; policies with empty sources that allow all callers still count as deployed but indicate weak granularity

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Linkerd mesh environments, check for ServerAuthorization and MeshTLSAuthentication resources that restrict inbound connections
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get serverauthorization,meshtlsauthentication --all-namespaces -o yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ServerAuthorization objects present with identityRef bindings confirm authorization controls are deployed in Linkerd

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the Kiali service mesh dashboard, navigate to the Istio Config section filtered to AuthorizationPolicy type to visually verify policies exist per namespace and review their rule structures
how_to_obtain.navigation: Kiali Dashboard > Istio Config > select 'AuthorizationPolicy' from the type filter > review entries per namespace and verify source principal bindings are present
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-empty list of AuthorizationPolicy entries across protected namespaces; namespaces with no entries indicate gaps in authorization enforcement

option_description: Controls the finest level of access control enforced in authorization policies between services — ranging from no policy, through namespace-wide rules, service-level rules, to method/endpoint-level rules specifying exact HTTP methods and URL paths per source service.
security_impact: The Rego rule `authorization_policy_granularity` only fires when `policy_granularity_level` is 'method' or 'service', combined with a default-deny policy and source principal binding. Coarser granularity (namespace or none) leaves overly broad access paths open between services, increasing blast radius if any single service is compromised. Method-level granularity is the strongest posture, ensuring a service can only call the specific endpoints it legitimately needs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all Istio AuthorizationPolicies across namespaces and inspect their `to` rules for HTTP method and path constraints
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, rules: .spec.rules}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policies with `to[].operation.methods` and `to[].operation.paths` arrays populated indicate method-level granularity; policies with only `to[].operation.hosts` indicate service-level; policies with only namespace `from` fields indicate namespace-level.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for OPA/Envoy RBAC filter configurations in the Envoy bootstrap or via istioctl proxy-config to identify method-level rules
how_to_obtain.command: istioctl proxy-config listener <pod-name>.<namespace> --port 15006 -o json | jq '.[].filterChains[].filters[] | select(.name=="envoy.filters.network.rbac") | .typedConfig'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RBAC policies with `principals`, `permissions.and_rules` containing `url_path` and `header` matchers confirm method-level enforcement at the proxy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review AuthorizationPolicy YAML manifests stored in version-controlled infrastructure repositories for the presence of `methods` and `paths` fields under `spec.rules[].to[].operation`
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'methods\|paths' ./k8s/authorizationpolicies/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of `methods: ["GET","POST"]` and `paths: ["/api/v1/resource"]` entries confirms method-level granularity.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the Istio Kiali dashboard, navigate to Graph > select a service > Outbound Traffic and inspect the authorization policy badges on edges to confirm method-level annotations are displayed
how_to_obtain.navigation: Kiali Dashboard → Graph → Namespace: <target> → Click service edge → Traffic tab → Check HTTP method breakdown
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Edge traffic breakdown shows per-method call counts consistent with method-level policy enforcement.

typical_values: service (common in teams with service-ownership models)

option_description: Indicates whether a default-deny AuthorizationPolicy or equivalent mechanism exists to block all inter-service traffic that is not explicitly permitted by an ALLOW rule, implementing an implicit-deny posture across the mesh.
security_impact: The Rego rule `authorization_policy_granularity` requires `default_deny_policy_present == true` as a mandatory condition alongside policy granularity and principal binding. Without a default-deny policy, any service can call any other service that lacks an explicit DENY rule, completely undermining the zero-trust model regardless of how fine-grained individual ALLOW policies are. Istio's security model depends on the presence of this baseline deny to activate policy enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search for namespace-wide or mesh-wide deny-all AuthorizationPolicies that have no `rules` field or an explicit `action: DENY` with empty `to`/`from`
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.action=="DENY" or (.spec.rules == null and .spec.action != "ALLOW")) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, action: .spec.action}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more policies returned with `action: DENY` and no restrictive `rules`, indicating a deny-all baseline. Empty output means no default-deny is present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test implicit deny behavior by attempting a call between two services that have no explicit ALLOW policy and verify it is rejected
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl exec -n <source-namespace> <source-pod> -- curl -sv http://<target-service>.<target-namespace>.svc.cluster.local:<port>/health 2>&1 | grep -E 'HTTP|RBAC|denied'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HTTP 403 or RBAC access denied response confirms default-deny is active. HTTP 200 without a policy indicates no default-deny.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review mesh-wide default policy in Istio MeshConfig or the `istio-system` namespace for a catch-all AuthorizationPolicy
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy -n istio-system -o yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A policy with `spec: {}` (no rules) when at least one ALLOW policy exists in the namespace, or `action: DENY` with no conditions, confirms default-deny.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform security team to confirm whether namespace isolation and default-deny were established as part of the mesh onboarding process, and request the relevant runbooks or Terraform/Helm configurations
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation or runbook explicitly referencing default-deny policy deployment as a prerequisite for service onboarding.

typical_values: false (majority of clusters without explicit zero-trust onboarding)
true (clusters following CIS Kubernetes or NIST SP 800-204 guidance)

option_description: Controls whether authorization policies use cryptographic service identities — specifically SPIFFE URIs carried in mTLS certificates (source.principal) or JWT claims — as the binding for access rules, rather than relying solely on IP addresses, namespace labels, or pod labels which can be spoofed or reused.
security_impact: The Rego rule `authorization_policy_granularity` requires `source_principal_binding_enforced == true` to qualify as a valid granularity countermeasure. IP-based or label-based rules can be circumvented by IP spoofing, pod label manipulation, or namespace label reassignment. Cryptographic binding to SPIFFE SVIDs ensures the identity asserted in policy matches a certificate-backed workload identity, making impersonation attacks significantly harder.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect AuthorizationPolicy `from[].source` fields across all namespaces to confirm `principals` (SPIFFE URI) are used rather than `ipBlocks` or only `namespaces`/`labels`
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, sources: [.spec.rules[]?.from[]?.source // empty]}' | jq 'select(.sources[].principals != null)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policies showing `principals: ["cluster.local/ns/<ns>/sa/<serviceaccount>"]` confirm SPIFFE-based binding. Policies showing only `namespaces` or `ipBlocks` indicate weaker binding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that the workload certificate SANs contain SPIFFE URIs by inspecting the proxy certificate for a running pod
how_to_obtain.command: istioctl proxy-config secret <pod-name>.<namespace> -o json | jq '.dynamicActiveSecrets[] | select(.name=="default") | .secret.tlsCertificate.certificateChain.inlineBytes' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -text | grep -A2 'Subject Alternative Name'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output containing `URI:spiffe://cluster.local/ns/<namespace>/sa/<serviceaccount>` confirms workloads are issued SPIFFE SVIDs that can be bound in policies.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review PeerAuthentication and AuthorizationPolicy YAML files to confirm `source.principal` fields reference SPIFFE URIs rather than wildcard namespace or IP ranges
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy --all-namespaces -o yaml | grep -A3 'source:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing `principals:` with `spiffe://` URIs or `cluster.local/ns/*/sa/*` patterns confirm cryptographic principal binding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the Istio Kiali dashboard, open the Security tab for a service and verify that mTLS is active and the source workload identity is displayed as a SPIFFE URI
how_to_obtain.navigation: Kiali Dashboard → Services → <service-name> → Overview tab → mTLS badge → click for certificate details
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SPIFFE URI displayed as the source identity for inbound connections confirms cryptographic principal binding is in effect.

typical_values: false (clusters using only namespace-based or label-based policies)
true (clusters with mTLS STRICT mode and SPIFFE-aware AuthorizationPolicies)

option_description: Describes the enforcement mode of service-level authorization policies — whether the system operates with deny-by-default (only explicitly permitted principals can invoke services), allow-by-default (all traffic permitted unless explicitly denied), or no policy configured at all.
security_impact: The Rego rule `unauthorized_call_prevention_coverage` requires `authorization_policy_mode == 'deny_by_default'` as a mandatory condition. Allow-by-default or not-configured modes mean any service within the mesh can call any other service without restriction, completely eliminating inter-service access control. Deny-by-default ensures that policy gaps result in blocked traffic rather than unauthorized access, aligning with the principle of least privilege.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Istio AuthorizationPolicy resources to determine whether ALLOW or DENY action is used as the baseline pattern across namespaces
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, action: (.spec.action // "ALLOW")}' | jq -s 'group_by(.action) | map({action: .[0].action, count: length})'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Summary showing count of DENY vs ALLOW policies. Predominantly ALLOW policies with a baseline DENY catch-all indicates deny_by_default. All ALLOW with no baseline DENY indicates allow_by_default.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the OPA/Envoy RBAC filter mode on a representative sidecar proxy to determine if it is operating in DENY or ALLOW default mode
how_to_obtain.command: istioctl proxy-config listener <pod-name>.<namespace> -o json | jq '.[].filterChains[].filters[] | select(.name=="envoy.filters.http.rbac") | .typedConfig.rules.action'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output of `DENY` means the RBAC filter denies unless matched (deny_by_default). Output of `ALLOW` or absent field means allow_by_default.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Istio MeshConfig or Helm values to identify the default authorization policy action configured at mesh initialization
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get configmap istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | grep -E 'authorizationPolicy|defaultConfig'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration entries referencing authorization policy defaults. Absence of explicit deny configuration may indicate allow_by_default or not_configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the Istio control plane dashboard (e.g., Grafana Istio mesh overview or Kiali) and examine the security posture panel for policy enforcement mode indicators
how_to_obtain.navigation: Kiali Dashboard → Overview → Namespace badges → Security indicator → AuthorizationPolicy status per namespace
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lock icons on all namespaces with AuthorizationPolicy enforcement active indicates deny_by_default posture. Unlocked namespaces indicate not_configured or allow_by_default.

option_description: Specifies where credential validation and authorization checks are performed relative to request processing — at the sidecar proxy/ingress layer before the application receives the request (proxy_layer), within application middleware before business logic executes (application_middleware), only after-the-fact via audit logs (post_hoc_audit_only), or not at all (none).
security_impact: The Rego rule `unauthorized_call_prevention_coverage` requires `pre_execution_enforcement_point` to be either 'proxy_layer' or 'application_middleware' — enforcement must occur before business logic processes the request to constitute prevention rather than detection. Post-hoc audit or no enforcement means unauthorized requests reach application code, enabling exploitation before any blocking occurs. Proxy_layer is the strongest option as it is independent of application code correctness.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify sidecar proxy injection status for all pods in target namespaces — only injected pods have proxy-layer enforcement
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, sidecar_injected: (.metadata.annotations["sidecar.istio.io/status"] != null)}' | jq 'select(.sidecar_injected == false)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Empty output means all pods have sidecar injection (proxy_layer enforcement available). Any returned pods are running without proxy enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm the Envoy RBAC filter is positioned before the router filter in the filter chain, ensuring enforcement occurs before the request is proxied to the application
how_to_obtain.command: istioctl proxy-config listener <pod-name>.<namespace> --port 15006 -o json | jq '.[].filterChains[].filters[] | .name'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Filter chain should show `envoy.filters.http.rbac` appearing before `envoy.filters.http.router`, confirming pre-execution enforcement at proxy layer.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether the application framework implements authentication middleware by reviewing deployment environment variables or application startup logs for middleware registration
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl logs <pod-name> -n <namespace> | grep -iE 'middleware|auth.*filter|interceptor|pre.*handler' | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries confirming middleware registration at application startup indicate application_middleware enforcement if proxy injection is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the namespace-level injection label and any per-pod annotation overrides that might disable sidecar injection, bypassing proxy-layer enforcement
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get namespace --show-labels | grep -v 'istio-injection=enabled'; kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.metadata.annotations["sidecar.istio.io/inject"]=="false") | {name:.metadata.name, namespace:.metadata.namespace}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Namespaces without `istio-injection=enabled` label or pods with inject=false annotation indicate proxy_layer enforcement is absent for those workloads.

typical_values: none (unmanaged clusters or namespaces without injection)
proxy_layer (fully injected namespaces with Istio STRICT mode)

option_description: Controls whether structured audit logging is enabled for all authentication attempts — both successful and failed — as they traverse service mesh boundaries, capturing the events at the sidecar proxy, ingress gateway, or policy engine level.
security_impact: The Rego rule `authentication_event_logging_completeness` requires `auth_event_logging_enabled == true` as its first condition. Without this logging, there is no forensic record of which services authenticated to which other services, making lateral movement reconstruction impossible after an incident. Authentication failures that could indicate credential abuse or brute-force attacks against service identities go undetected.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Istio Telemetry resource configuration to confirm access logging is explicitly enabled for all workloads
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get telemetry --all-namespaces -o yaml | grep -A10 'accessLogging'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Telemetry resources with `accessLogging` providers configured (e.g., `- providers: [{name: envoy}]`) confirm auth event logging is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify Envoy access log output from a sidecar proxy by examining a recent request and confirming auth-related fields are captured in the access log stream
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl logs <pod-name> -n <namespace> -c istio-proxy | tail -20 | jq '{method: .method, response_code: .response_code, upstream_host: .upstream_host, authority: .authority}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Structured JSON log entries for each request confirm access logging is active. Empty output or plain-text unstructured logs indicate logging is disabled or misconfigured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the Istio MeshConfig for the `accessLogFile` or `accessLogEncoding` settings that control global access log output
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get configmap istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | grep -E 'accessLog|telemetry'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: `accessLogFile: /dev/stdout` and `accessLogEncoding: JSON` entries confirm structured access logging enabled globally.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the centralized log aggregation system (e.g., Elasticsearch, Splunk, Cloud Logging) for auth event log entries from the service mesh within the past 24 hours
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl logs -n istio-system -l app=istiod --since=1h | grep -E 'auth|mTLS|certificate|RBAC' | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-zero count of authentication-related log entries confirms that auth events are being generated and flowing to log infrastructure.

typical_values: false (default Istio installation without explicit telemetry configuration)
true (deployments following CIS Istio benchmark or SOC2/PCI compliance requirements)

option_description: Indicates the completeness of required fields captured in authentication event log entries — specifically source service identity (SPIFFE URI or certificate CN), destination service name, ISO 8601 timestamp, and policy decision outcome (allow/deny). Rated as full (all four present), partial (some missing), or none (logging absent or fields not captured).
security_impact: The Rego rule `authentication_event_logging_completeness` requires `logged_fields_coverage == 'full'` alongside auth event logging being enabled. Partial or no field coverage means forensic investigations cannot reliably reconstruct which service identity made a request to which target, when it occurred, and whether it was permitted or denied — the four essential data points for lateral movement analysis. Missing policy outcome fields specifically prevent detection of repeated RBAC denials indicating reconnaissance.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Sample recent Envoy access log entries from a sidecar proxy and verify all four required fields are present: source identity, destination, timestamp, and response code
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl logs <pod-name> -n <namespace> -c istio-proxy --since=10m | head -5 | python3 -c "import sys,json; [print({k: json.loads(l).get(k,'MISSING') for k in ['authority','upstream_host','start_time','response_code','x-forwarded-client-cert']}) for l in sys.stdin]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All five keys populated with non-null values: `authority` (destination), `upstream_host` (target service), `start_time` (ISO timestamp), `response_code` (policy outcome), `x-forwarded-client-cert` (source identity). Any `MISSING` value indicates partial coverage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that the Envoy access log format string includes the `%DOWNSTREAM_PEER_URI_SAN%` field to capture SPIFFE URI from the client certificate
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get configmap istio -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | python3 -c "import sys,yaml; cfg=yaml.safe_load(sys.stdin.read()); print(cfg.get('accessLogFormat','NOT_SET'))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log format string containing `%DOWNSTREAM_PEER_URI_SAN%`, `%REQ(:authority)%`, `%START_TIME%`, and `%RESPONSE_CODE%` confirms full field coverage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the centralized logging system for a sample of authentication event logs and verify all four required fields are populated across different source services
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl logs -l app=<service-name> -n <namespace> -c istio-proxy --since=1h | jq -r '[.start_time, .upstream_host, .response_code, .downstream_peer_uri_san] | @csv' | head -10
how_to_obtain.expected_output: CSV rows with all four columns populated for every entry confirm full coverage. Empty columns in any row indicate partial coverage for that log source.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the Istio Telemetry resource's `accessLogging` provider configuration to confirm a structured log format with the required fields is specified
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get telemetry -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A30 'accessLogging'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Telemetry resource specifying a custom access log format or referencing a provider (e.g., OpenTelemetry, Stackdriver) configured with source identity, destination, timestamp, and policy outcome fields.

typical_values: none (access logging disabled or not structured)
partial (timestamp and destination present but SPIFFE identity or policy outcome missing)
full (all four required fields present in structured JSON access logs)

option_description: Controls whether authentication failure events—such as rejected mTLS handshakes, certificate validation errors, and policy-denied service calls—are explicitly written to audit logs alongside successful authentication events.
security_impact: The Rego rule `authentication_event_logging_completeness` requires `failure_events_captured == true` alongside `auth_event_logging_enabled == true` and `logged_fields_coverage == 'full'` to award the countermeasure score. Without failure event logging, lateral movement attempts that generate rejected calls leave no forensic trace, making it impossible to reconstruct attack paths or detect brute-force service impersonation attempts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Istio's Telemetry API to check whether access log providers are configured to capture denied requests. Look for a Telemetry resource that sets access logging mode to include errors.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get telemetry -A -o yaml | grep -A 10 'accessLogging'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A Telemetry resource with an accessLogging block; verify the filter expression does not exclude response_code >= 400 or that no filter is applied, meaning all events including denials are logged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Istio AuthorizationPolicy audit annotation settings or mesh config to confirm audit logging of deny actions is active.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get meshconfig -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -i 'accessLogFile\|accessLogEncoding\|enableTracing'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: accessLogFile set to '/dev/stdout' or a sink path, and no filtering that would suppress 4xx/5xx responses.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Simulate a denied service call by sending a request from a service with an invalid or missing certificate and then inspect the Envoy proxy access logs to confirm a deny log entry with policy outcome appears.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl logs -n <namespace> <pod-name> -c istio-proxy | grep '"response_code":403\|RBAC: access denied\|peer certificate\|upstream_reset'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log lines containing response code 403 or RBAC denial messages with source principal, destination, and timestamp fields present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect OPA or SPIRE audit configuration files to verify that denial outcomes are emitted as log events when those systems are used as the authorization decision point.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A decision_logs block with `console: true` or a remote service configured, and no filter that excludes `result == false` decisions.

option_description: Controls whether the service mesh or workload identity system is actively integrated with a certificate authority or PKI backend—such as Istio's Citadel/istiod with an external CA, cert-manager with Vault or AWS PCA, or SPIFFE/SPIRE with an upstream CA—so that service certificates are issued automatically rather than manually provisioned.
security_impact: The Rego rule `certificate_lifecycle_management_integration` requires `ca_integration_enabled == true` as its first condition. Without CA integration, certificates must be manually issued and distributed, creating operational gaps where expired or missing certificates cause service outages or, worse, force operators to disable mTLS enforcement entirely. Automated CA integration is the prerequisite for both automatic rotation and revocation propagation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether istiod is configured to use an external CA by inspecting the mounted CA certificate secret and the EXTERNAL_CA or PILOT_CERT_PROVIDER environment variables.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get deploy istiod -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].env}' | python3 -m json.tool | grep -i 'cert_provider\|external_ca\|ca_addr'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Environment variables showing PILOT_CERT_PROVIDER set to 'custom' or a CA address pointing to Vault, cert-manager, or another PKI endpoint.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List cert-manager Certificate and ClusterIssuer resources to confirm an issuer is configured and actively issuing certificates to workloads.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterissuer,issuer,certificate -A -o wide
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ClusterIssuer or Issuer resources in READY=True state, and Certificate resources with READY=True and a recent EXPIRATION date, indicating active automated issuance.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For SPIFFE/SPIRE deployments, verify the SPIRE server is running and agents are attesting workloads by checking registered entries.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl exec -n spire deploy/spire-server -- /opt/spire/bin/spire-server entry show
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of SPIFFE ID entries mapping workload selectors to service identities, confirming SPIRE CA integration is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the istiod ConfigMap for the meshConfig.ca settings or check the IstioOperator resource for CA configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: meshConfig block containing caAddress or caCertificates fields pointing to an external PKI, or defaultConfig showing certificate provider settings.

option_description: Controls whether service workload certificates are configured to rotate automatically before their expiry—without human intervention—via mechanisms such as cert-manager's renewBefore field, Vault PKI's auto-renew lease, or SPIRE's agent rotation interval settings.
security_impact: The Rego rule `certificate_lifecycle_management_integration` requires `automatic_rotation_configured == true` alongside CA integration and a non-'none' revocation mechanism. Manual certificate rotation introduces windows where expired certificates either break service communication or are left in place past expiry. Automated rotation ensures the cryptographic identity underpinning mTLS remains continuously valid and limits the exposure window of any compromised certificate.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect cert-manager Certificate resources for a renewBefore field, which controls how far before expiry the certificate is automatically rotated.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get certificate -A -o yaml | grep -E 'renewBefore|duration|rotationPolicy'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Certificate specs with renewBefore set (e.g., '360h' or '24h'), indicating automatic renewal is configured ahead of certificate expiry.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the SPIRE agent configuration for the svid_ttl and rotation interval to confirm SVIDs are rotated automatically.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get configmap spire-agent -n spire -o yaml | grep -E 'svid_ttl|default_svid_ttl|rotation'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: svid_ttl set to a short duration (e.g., '1h') and agent configured to renew at half-TTL, confirming automatic rotation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Istio with its built-in CA, verify the workload certificate TTL and rotation check interval in the proxy configuration.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get configmap istio -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -E 'secretTTL|workloadCertTtl|certSignerDomain'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: workloadCertTtl set to a finite duration (default 24h in Istio), with proxies automatically fetching new certificates before expiry.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform team or review runbooks to determine whether any manual certificate renewal process exists, which would indicate automatic rotation is not fully configured.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No manual renewal runbooks or calendar reminders for certificate renewal; all renewal handled by automation with alerts only for rotation failures.

option_description: Identifies the method by which certificate revocation information is distributed to service mesh proxies and workloads when a certificate must be invalidated before its natural expiry. Options are CRL (Certificate Revocation List), OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol stapling), short-lived certificates where revocation is implicit due to brief TTL, push-based bundle updates (as used by SPIFFE/SPIRE), or none.
security_impact: The Rego rule `certificate_lifecycle_management_integration` requires that `revocation_propagation_mechanism` is NOT 'none' for the countermeasure to apply. Without a revocation mechanism, a compromised service certificate remains valid until its scheduled expiry, giving an attacker an uninterrupted window to impersonate that service across mTLS connections. The choice of mechanism also affects latency of revocation propagation and operational complexity.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check SPIRE server bundle configuration and federation settings to determine whether push-based bundle updates are being used for implicit revocation.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl exec -n spire deploy/spire-server -- /opt/spire/bin/spire-server bundle show -format spiffe
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A SPIFFE trust bundle output; combined with short SVID TTL (< 24h), this indicates short_lived_implicit or push_based revocation is in use.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the cert-manager Issuer or Vault PKI role configuration for OCSP or CRL settings to identify the revocation distribution method.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterissuer -A -o yaml | grep -E 'ocsp|crl|revocation'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Fields such as ocsp_servers, crl_distribution_points, or generate_lease indicating which revocation mechanism the PKI backend publishes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect actual issued service certificates to read the embedded CRL Distribution Points or OCSP extension to determine what mechanism is encoded.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl exec -n <namespace> <pod> -c istio-proxy -- openssl x509 -in /var/run/secrets/istio/cert-chain.pem -noout -text | grep -A 3 'CRL\|OCSP\|Authority Information'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: X.509 extensions showing either a CRL distribution point URL, an OCSP responder URI, or absence of both (indicating short-lived implicit revocation).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review PKI architecture documentation or interview the security infrastructure team to determine the intended revocation strategy and whether it has been validated end-to-end.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation explicitly naming the revocation mechanism (CRL, OCSP, short-lived, push-based) with evidence it has been tested for propagation latency.

option_description: Controls whether authorization policies—such as Istio AuthorizationPolicy manifests, OPA Rego files, or SPIFFE/SPIRE registration entry definitions—are stored in a version control system like Git, enabling change history, peer review, and rollback rather than being applied ad-hoc directly to the cluster.
security_impact: The Rego rule `policy_as_code_maintainability` requires `authorization_policies_version_controlled == true` as its mandatory first condition for both rule branches. Without version control, policy changes cannot be audited, reviewed, or rolled back, creating risk of undocumented permissive changes that expand the attack surface across service mesh boundaries. Version control is the foundation enabling GitOps-based policy governance.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Ask the platform or security team to demonstrate the repository where authorization policies are stored and show a recent commit history including policy change commits.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A Git repository (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, etc.) containing AuthorizationPolicy YAML or OPA Rego files with a meaningful commit history showing changes over time.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether currently deployed Istio AuthorizationPolicy resources contain Git-related annotations (e.g., from Flux or ArgoCD) indicating they were applied from a repository.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy -A -o yaml | grep -E 'argocd.argoproj.io|kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io|git.commit|managed-by'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Annotations such as kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/name or argocd.argoproj.io/app on AuthorizationPolicy resources, confirming GitOps-managed deployment from a version-controlled source.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the team's source control platform (GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket) and search for repositories containing Kubernetes YAML files or OPA policies used for service mesh authorization.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitHub → Organization → Repositories → Search for 'AuthorizationPolicy' or 'istio' or 'opa' in repository contents; verify policy files exist with commit history.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more repositories containing policy files with a meaningful commit log showing who changed which policy and when.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Look for ArgoCD Application or Flux GitRepository/Kustomization resources that reference authorization policy paths in a Git source.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get application -n argocd -o yaml | grep -E 'repoURL|path|targetRevision'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ArgoCD Application specs with repoURL pointing to a Git repository and a path that includes policy manifests, confirming version-controlled deployment source.

option_description: Controls whether authorization policies are deployed exclusively through an automated CI/CD pipeline—such as GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, ArgoCD, or Flux—preventing direct manual application via kubectl or direct API access to the cluster, which would bypass review and audit gates.
security_impact: The Rego rule `policy_as_code_maintainability` requires `cicd_pipeline_enforces_policy_deployment == true` in both its branches. Manual policy application bypasses peer review, testing, and audit trail, creating risk that unauthorized or misconfigured policies are silently deployed. CI/CD enforcement ensures every policy change passes through defined gates before reaching production workloads, reducing configuration drift and insider risk.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect ArgoCD Application sync settings or Flux Kustomization resources to verify they are set to auto-sync from Git, meaning no manual kubectl apply is necessary or effective.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get kustomization -A -o yaml | grep -E 'syncPolicy|automated|prune|selfHeal'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Kustomization or ArgoCD Application resources with automated sync and selfHeal: true, meaning the cluster continuously reconciles to the Git state and manual changes are reverted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the CI/CD pipeline definition files for stages that apply authorization policies and confirm there are deploy stages calling kubectl apply or helm upgrade.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitHub → Repository → .github/workflows/ OR GitLab → Repository → .gitlab-ci.yml → Look for job steps that run kubectl apply -f policies/ or helm upgrade with policy values.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pipeline YAML files containing explicit policy deployment steps with environment-specific gates (approval, test pass) before deployment executes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify with the platform team that direct cluster access (kubectl) for policy changes is restricted via RBAC and that no runbooks describe manual policy application as a standard procedure.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o yaml | grep -E 'kubectl\|admin\|cluster-admin' | grep -v system:
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No broad cluster-admin bindings for human users; service accounts used only by CI/CD tools have apply permissions, while human users are limited to read-only or namespaced roles.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for branch protection rules and required CI checks in the version control platform that prevent direct merges to main/production branch without pipeline success.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitHub → Repository → Settings → Branches → Branch protection rules → Verify 'Require status checks to pass before merging' is enabled for the production branch.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Branch protection rules requiring at least one CI status check (policy lint, test, security scan) to pass before merges that would trigger policy deployment.

option_description: Controls whether automated policy validation and unit testing—using tools such as OPA conftest, Rego unit tests (opa test), Kyverno policy tests, or policy linting tools—are executed as mandatory pipeline stages before authorization policies are deployed to any environment.
security_impact: The Rego rule `policy_as_code_maintainability` uses this attribute as a differentiator between its two branches: the stronger branch (higher assurance) requires all three conditions including `policy_testing_integrated_in_pipeline == true`. Without automated testing, syntactically valid but semantically incorrect policies can be deployed—for example, an overly permissive default-allow rule introduced accidentally—exposing internal services to unauthorized callers before the error is noticed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect CI pipeline definition files for test stages invoking conftest, opa test, or policy linting commands against the authorization policy files.
how_to_obtain.command: find . -name '*.yml' -o -name '*.yaml' | xargs grep -l 'conftest\|opa test\|kyverno test\|policy.*lint' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more pipeline files containing stages or jobs that run conftest verify, opa test, or equivalent tools against the policies directory before the deploy stage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the repository for test files co-located with policy files, such as OPA test files ending in _test.rego or conftest test suites.
how_to_obtain.command: find . -name '*_test.rego' -o -name 'conftest.toml' -o -name 'policy-test*' | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of _test.rego files, a conftest.toml configuration, or dedicated test subdirectories alongside the main policy files, indicating testing infrastructure exists.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the CI/CD pipeline run history and inspect a recent pipeline execution to confirm a policy test stage ran and produced pass/fail output before the deploy stage.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitHub Actions → Repository → Actions tab → Select latest workflow run for a policy change → Expand job steps → Look for a 'Policy Test' or 'conftest' step with green status.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A completed pipeline run showing a distinct policy validation step with output from conftest or opa test indicating passes/failures, positioned before any deployment step.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Ask the team responsible for service mesh policy management whether they have written unit tests for authorization policies and whether failing tests block deployments.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation that test failures cause pipeline failure and block deployment, with examples of test cases covering both allowed and denied call scenarios.

option_description: Controls whether a formal, documented expected service-to-service communication topology has been defined—specifying which services are permitted to call which other services—and whether this baseline is actively enforced or used as a reference for anomaly detection within the service mesh.
security_impact: The Rego rule `anomalous_call_pattern_detection` requires `baseline_communication_graph_defined == true` as its mandatory first condition in both branches. Without a defined communication graph, there is no authoritative reference against which to identify unexpected lateral calls—a key indicator of compromised service accounts or lateral movement. The graph serves as the ground truth for both policy enforcement and runtime anomaly alerting.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect all Istio AuthorizationPolicy resources across namespaces to determine whether they collectively describe a complete allowed communication topology between services.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get authorizationpolicy -A -o yaml | python3 -c "import sys,yaml; docs=list(yaml.safe_load_all(sys.stdin)); [print(d.get('metadata',{}).get('namespace',''),d.get('metadata',{}).get('name',''),d.get('spec',{}).get('rules',[])) for d in docs if d]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A set of AuthorizationPolicy resources with explicit source principal selectors defining which service accounts or namespaces may call each destination service, covering all production services.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Look for a service dependency map or communication graph document in the repository (e.g., a network policy diagram, service mesh topology file, or architecture-as-code definition).
how_to_obtain.command: find . -name 'service-graph*' -o -name 'communication-matrix*' -o -name 'network-topology*' -o -name 'service-dependencies*' | head -10
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more files describing allowed service-to-service relationships, whether as YAML policy files, draw.io diagrams exported to JSON, or a structured dependency matrix.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for Linkerd ServiceProfiles or similar mesh-specific resources that define expected traffic routes, which can serve as a baseline communication graph.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get serviceprofile -A -o yaml | grep -E 'name:|routes:|isRetryable:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ServiceProfile resources defining expected routes per service, which collectively represent the baseline allowed communication patterns.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the service mesh observability dashboard (Kiali for Istio, or Linkerd Viz) to see if a traffic graph has been reviewed, validated, and exported as a policy baseline.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Kiali Dashboard → Graph → Namespace: All → Set time range to 7 days → Review displayed service graph → Check if the graph matches documented expected topology and whether AuthorizationPolicies reflect these edges.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A service graph where every displayed edge corresponds to an authorized call relationship defined in policy, with no unexpected edges that lack corresponding AuthorizationPolicy rules.

option_description: Controls the operational mode of the anomalous call pattern detection system within the service mesh or associated security tooling. Determines whether the detection engine actively blocks requests that deviate from the expected service communication graph ('enforcing'), only generates alerts for review ('alerting'), or is completely inactive ('disabled').
security_impact: This attribute is a direct input to the `anomalous_call_pattern_detection` Rego rule. The rule fires — and the countermeasure is credited — only when `anomaly_detection_mode` is either 'enforcing' or 'alerting'. A value of 'disabled' means lateral movement between services that violates the expected communication graph will go undetected and unblocked, providing no runtime defense against a compromised microservice pivoting to unauthorized peers. Setting this to 'enforcing' provides the strongest posture by actively blocking anomalous calls before execution; 'alerting' enables forensic visibility but leaves traffic unblocked.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Istio telemetry or Envoy-based detection pipeline configuration to identify the current anomaly detection enforcement mode. If using Istio with a custom WASM plugin or OPA-Envoy integration, inspect the deployed ConfigMap that governs detection behavior.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get configmap -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A 5 -i 'anomaly_detection_mode\|detection_mode\|enforcement_mode'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A key-value pair such as `anomaly_detection_mode: enforcing` or `detection_mode: alerting` within the ConfigMap data block.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the service mesh policy configuration file or the SIEM detection engine rule definition that governs anomalous call pattern behavior. For Istio deployments this is often a custom EnvoyFilter or Telemetry resource; for Falco-based pipelines check the rules file.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A rule block containing a field such as `- rule: Anomalous Service Call` with an `output:` (alerting) or `warn_after:` / `block:` directive (enforcing), or absence of the rule entirely (disabled).

how_to_obtain.instruction: If using a service mesh management plane API (e.g., Istio pilot-discovery or a service mesh gateway admin API), query the active policy objects to determine the current anomaly detection enforcement state.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get envoyfilter,telemetry -n istio-system -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, mode: .spec}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output listing deployed EnvoyFilter or Telemetry objects; look for fields indicating 'ENFORCE', 'LOG_ONLY', or absence of the resource entirely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the Kiali service mesh observability dashboard, navigate to the Graph view and open the 'Security' panel or the 'Traffic Policies' section to inspect whether anomaly detection enforcement is shown as active, passive, or unconfigured.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Kiali UI → Graph → Namespace selector → Display → Security → Review 'Anomaly Detection' policy status badge per service node
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A status indicator showing 'Enforcing', 'Alerting / Monitor Only', or no indicator (disabled) next to relevant service nodes.

option_description: Indicates whether authentication and authorization events emitted by the service mesh (mTLS handshake outcomes, Envoy RBAC policy decisions, SPIFFE/SVID validation results) are being actively ingested into a SIEM or detection pipeline and correlated in real time or near-real time against a defined baseline service communication graph to identify unexpected peer relationships.
security_impact: This boolean is a required input in both branches of the `anomalous_call_pattern_detection` Rego rule — the rule cannot satisfy either condition unless `auth_event_correlation_enabled == true`. Without event correlation, even if a baseline communication graph is defined and a detection mode is configured, the system has no data feed to compare against and the anomalous call pattern detection countermeasure receives no credit. Enabling this ensures that every mTLS handshake and authorization policy decision is captured, forwarded to a correlation engine, and continuously compared against expected service-to-service communication patterns, enabling detection of compromised service principals attempting to invoke unauthorized endpoints.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that Istio access logging and telemetry export are enabled for the mesh and that logs are being forwarded to a SIEM or detection pipeline. Check for the presence of a Telemetry resource that captures auth-related fields.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get telemetry -A -o yaml | grep -E 'accessLogging|providers|meshConfig' && kubectl -n istio-system get configmap istio -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | grep -E 'enableTracing|accessLogFile|accessLogEncoding'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing `accessLogging` enabled with a provider such as `stackdriver`, `otel`, or `envoy`; `accessLogFile` pointing to a log sink; and/or a named telemetry provider exporting to a SIEM pipeline.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm that auth events (mTLS peer authentication outcomes and RBAC decision logs) are actively arriving in the SIEM by querying recent ingestion for service mesh authentication log types.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'response_flags|peer_principal|upstream_host|rbac_access' /var/log/envoy/access.log | tail -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Recent log lines containing fields such as `peer_principal=spiffe://cluster.local/ns/default/sa/frontend`, `rbac_access=allowed|denied`, and `response_flags=-` or `rbac`, confirming structured auth events are being captured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM or detection pipeline API (e.g., Elasticsearch, Splunk, or Datadog) to verify that service mesh authentication events are being ingested and that a correlation rule referencing the service communication graph is active.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -X GET 'http://localhost:9200/service-mesh-auth-events-*/_search?size=1&sort=@timestamp:desc' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' | jq '.hits.hits[0]._source | {timestamp: ."@timestamp", peer_principal, rbac_decision}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A JSON document showing a recent auth event with `peer_principal`, `rbac_decision`, and timestamp fields populated, confirming active ingestion from the service mesh telemetry pipeline.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform security or observability team to confirm that a correlation rule mapping observed service-to-service auth events against a defined baseline communication graph is deployed and active in the SIEM or detection engine, and that the rule is not in a paused or draft state.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SIEM Console (e.g., Splunk / Elastic SIEM / Chronicle) → Detection Rules → Search 'service mesh peer' or 'mtls correlation' → Confirm rule status is 'Active/Enabled' and review last triggered timestamp
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A confirmed active detection rule that references service mesh auth event fields, with a last-triggered timestamp indicating recent execution, and a documented mapping to the expected service communication graph.
